raw_case_text:
The patient, a 58-year-old menopausal woman and farmer with a 10-year history of depression and uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus until this examination, reported experiencing vulvar itching for 5 days. She was admitted to the 103 Military Medical Hospital (Hanoi, Vietnam) on November 28, 2019, with complaints of vulvar itching and vaginal discharge. Physical examination of the vagina revealed thin white exudate on the vulvar structures, an odor, and vulvar itching. Due to the suspected diagnosis of vulvovaginitis caused by the Candida, 2 vaginal swab specimens were collected using sterile cotton-tipped swab. These vaginal swabs were promptly transported to the Department of Medical Parasitology at Vietnam Military Medical University in Ha Noi, Vietnam, within 2 hours for yeast isolation. Examination results with 10% KOH revealed the presence of oval yeast. In addition, the vaginal swab sample was also cultured on CHROMagar Candida plates and incubated at 20 C to 25 C and 35 C for 4 days. After 2 days of culturing at 20 C to 25 C, mauve colonies emerged, displaying smooth, glossy, slim characteristics and a diameter of 0.5 to 1 mm, making them indistinguished from Candida glabrata colonies (Figure 1). Examination under the microscope of the culture after 48 hours indicated oval yeast, ranging in size from 3 to 5 microm in length to 2 to 3 microm in diameter, either single or in clusters without true hyphae or pseudohyphae (Figure 2). No growth was observed on CHROMagar Candida at 35 C. Subsequently, a subculture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) (Merck, Germany) was performed, and it was incubated at 20 C to 25 C for 48 hours. The cream-colored colonies produced were slightly mucoid and highly glossy (Figure 3A). After 3 days, the color changed to a pale yellow-pink shade (Figure 3B). Complete blood count and liver function tests were performed, and all results were within the normal range. Serological assessments for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV were negative. However, her fasting blood glucose concentration was 9.13 mmol/L. The isolated yeast was then amplified and sequenced using the ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 region as described previously.   The fungus was identified as C victoriae using the BLAST tool and the sequence was deposited in the GenBank under accession number MW307706.1.
Susceptibility testing of the isolation to amphotericin B (AMB), caspofungin (CAS), micafungin (MFG), fluconazole (FLC), itraconazole (ICZ), and voriconazole (VCZ) was carried out according to the recommendations proposed by the Clinical and Laboratory Standard Institute (CLSI) document M27-A3.   The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values for AMB, CAS, MFG, FLC, ICZ, and VCZ were 1 mug/mL, 0.12 mug/mL, 0.015 mug/mL, 0.12 mug/mL, 0.06 mug/mL, and 0.015 mug/mL, respectively.
The patient was treated with topical clotrimazole and then received 200 mg of itraconazole daily for 7 days. Blood glucose levels were maintained within normal limits with 500 mg of Glucophage XR (Merck, Germany) 3 times a day. The 1-month treatment completely resolved the vulvar lesions, and no presence of yeast was observed in the samples of vaginal discharge after 1, 3, and 6 months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old menopausal female farmer presented with a 5-day history of vulvar itching and vaginal discharge.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the hospital on November 28, 2019, reporting 5 days of persistent vulvar pruritus accompanied by abnormal vaginal discharge.
subjective.past_medical_history: 10-year history of depression and uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus; menopausal; farmer by occupation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for vulvar itching and malodorous vaginal discharge.

objective.physical_examination: Pelvic and vulvar examination revealed thin white exudate on the vulvar structures, malodor, and signs of vulvar pruritus.
objective.routine_investigations: Fasting blood glucose was elevated at 9.13 mmol/L; complete blood count and liver function tests were within normal limits; serologies for HBV, HCV, and HIV were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Direct microscopy of vaginal swab specimens with 10% KOH showed oval yeast cells (3-5 um x 2-3 um) without hyphae or pseudohyphae. Culture on CHROMagar Candida and Sabouraud dextrose agar at 20-25 C (no growth at 35 C) yielded glossy mauve/cream-to-pinkish mucoid colonies.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of vulvovaginitis caused by Cryptococcus (Vishniacozyma) victoriae in a patient with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus, confirmed by vaginal swab fungal culture at 20-25 C and ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 rDNA sequencing with BLAST identification (GenBank accession MW307706.1) and CLSI M27-A3 antifungal susceptibility testing (MICs: amphotericin B 1 ug/mL, caspofungin 0.12 ug/mL, micafungin 0.015 ug/mL, fluconazole 0.12 ug/mL, itraconazole 0.06 ug/mL, voriconazole 0.015 ug/mL). Treated with topical clotrimazole, oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 7 days, and metformin XR (Glucophage XR 500 mg three times daily) for glycemic control, achieving complete clinical and mycological resolution at 1, 3, and 6 months of follow-up.
